guides.title: Fire Starting Methods
guides.summary: Fire starting is a sequence problem: dry fuel, protected ignition, airflow, and safety discipline matter more than any single gadget.
steps: Build fuel in stages: tinder, kindling, and larger fuel before striking ignition.
Protect the fire lay from wind and ground moisture before using matches, lighter, or ferro rod.
Light the tinder first and feed the flame gradually with smaller fuel.
Keep water, soil, or another extinguishing method ready before the fire grows.
guides.notes: Observe total fire bans, local restrictions, and bushfire conditions. Do not light open flame where fire risk is high or prohibited.

guides.title: Water Collection Basics
guides.summary: Collecting water is about finding the cleanest source first, then moving it safely into storage before treatment.
steps: Use the highest and cleanest source available before resorting to stagnant or flood-affected water.
Keep raw water containers separate from treated drinking water containers.
Pre-filter dirty water through cloth or settling before full treatment.
Treat collected water before drinking unless the source is already trusted and protected.
guides.notes: Floodwater and industrial runoff can remain unsafe after basic filtration. Choose source quality before volume whenever possible.

guides.title: Rainwater Harvesting Setup
guides.summary: Rainwater harvesting works best when roof catchment, first-flush diversion, and storage hygiene are handled before heavy rain arrives.
steps: Inspect roof, gutters, and screens before the wet season so debris does not foul the catchment.
Use a first-flush or discard the first dirty runoff where possible.
Store water in covered, food-safe containers or tanks that reduce light and contamination.
Label stored rainwater clearly and decide in advance whether it is for garden, washing, or treated drinking use.
guides.notes: Roof contamination, animal droppings, and ash can make rainwater unsafe. Reassess after storms, smoke, and long dry periods.

guides.title: Solar Cooking Basics
guides.summary: Solar cooking is slow and weather-dependent, but it can stretch fuel reserves when skies are clear and safe food temperatures are maintained.
steps: Use a reflective cooker or insulated dark pot setup in a stable sunny location.
Start early in the day and plan for longer cook times than gas or fire.
Keep lids on and avoid opening the cooker often so heat can build.
Confirm food is thoroughly cooked before eating, especially meat, beans, and reheated leftovers.
guides.notes: Solar cooking is not suitable for every weather condition. Have a backup method for unsafe temperatures or overcast days.

guides.title: Off-Grid Power Basics
guides.summary: Off-grid power planning starts with load reduction first, then matching batteries, solar input, and charging order to what actually matters.
steps: List critical loads first such as lights, phone charging, medical devices, and radio.
Reduce demand before adding batteries or panels by switching off high-draw devices.
Charge in priority order so communication and medical gear stay online longest.
Keep cables, power banks, adapters, and stored energy labelled and tested before outages.
guides.notes: Do not run combustion generators indoors or near openings. Carbon monoxide kills quickly in enclosed spaces.

guides.title: Shelter Building Basics
guides.summary: Emergency shelter is mainly about wind protection, insulation from the ground, drainage, and keeping work simple enough to finish before dark.
steps: Choose higher ground that avoids flood paths, dead branches, and exposed ridgelines.
Block wind first with tarp, vehicle, terrain, or vegetation before worrying about comfort.
Insulate the ground layer with dry material so body heat is not lost downward.
Keep the shelter low, stable, and easy to repair with the materials you already have.
guides.notes: Do not build in dry creek beds, under unstable trees, or where you cannot evacuate quickly if weather worsens.

guides.title: Food Preservation Without Grid Power
guides.summary: During outages, preserving food starts with triage: eat what spoils first, reduce repeated warming, and switch to drying, pickling, or high-salt methods where appropriate.
steps: Keep fridge and freezer doors closed and move quickly through the most perishable foods first.
Cook vulnerable foods early if safe heat is available, then consume or preserve them promptly.
Use drying, pickling, high-salt curing, or jam-making only when you already know the method and have clean gear.
Discard food that has been warm too long, smells wrong, or shows spoilage.
guides.notes: When in doubt, throw it out. Food poisoning during a disaster creates a second emergency.
